text: Four platforms show up again and again in real SOC job postings and real production environments: Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, and the Elastic Stack. This lesson doesn't teach you to click through any one of them -- it's a practical, honest overview of what each is actually known for, so you can talk about them accurately and know what you're walking into whichever one a future employer runs.

Splunk is one of the longest-standing enterprise SIEM platforms, built around SPL -- its own powerful search language -- with broad adoption across large enterprises. Microsoft Sentinel is Microsoft's cloud-native SIEM, built directly on Azure and queried with KQL, tightly integrated with Microsoft 365 Defender. IBM QRadar has a long track record in large enterprise and government environments, known for grouping related correlated events into what it calls an 'offense.' The Elastic Stack has open-source roots -- Elasticsearch, Logstash, Beats, and Kibana -- and can run as general log analytics or, with Elastic Security added, as a full SIEM.

The platforms differ mostly in their query language and deployment model, not in the underlying job. Searching for traffic from one IP address in Splunk's SPL looks like index equals firewall, source IP equals that address, piped into stats count by destination IP. The same question in Sentinel's KQL looks like SecurityEvent, where IP address equals that address, summarize count by computer. Different syntax, same underlying question -- which is exactly why the concepts from this chapter transfer across all of them.

This course stays vendor-neutral on purpose. Aggregation, normalization, correlation, and alerting work the same way conceptually no matter which platform runs them, and that's the foundation worth having solid before specializing. This path's very next course goes deep on one platform specifically -- Microsoft Sentinel -- with hands-on configuration and real detections.
Chapter 3 moves from platforms to the raw material every one of them ingests: the actual log formats, starting with syslog -- the oldest standard still running almost everywhere.
